sections.title: Page 7

summary.text: Introduces the guidelines, explaining that they are intended for policy-makers and planners in health and social services to help them develop policies supporting HIV/AIDS counselling services. It notes they may also interest managers and clinicians involved in policy-making.

sections.extract: WHO/GPA/TCO/HCS/95. 15 INTRODUCTION Who is this document intended for? These guidelines are intended to provide policy-makers and planners working in health and social service organizations! with information to enable them to develop policies that will stimulate, encourage and support the development of appropriate HIV/AIDS counselling services and plan for this service. This document presents general policy issues

sections.title: Page 8

summary.text: Lists policy issues the guidelines address, such as defining who qualifies as a counsellor and preparing staff for a new activity. It outlines the document's structure and refers to related WHO/GPA publications.

sections.extract: Counselling for HIV/AIDS: A key to caring - Carefully devised policies establishing who qualifies to be an HIV/AIDS counsellor are required. - Within most health and social services, HIV/AIDS counselling is a relatively new activity and, as such, may meet with different reactions from staff and supervisors. In order to avoid serious negative reactions, policy guidance and approval is needed as to the role and scope

sections.title: Page 9

summary.text: Opens Part One by giving the Global Programme on AIDS definition of HIV/AIDS counselling as a confidential dialogue that helps clients cope with stress and make personal decisions. It describes the components, including personal risk assessment and planning to reduce risk.

sections.extract: WHO/GPA/TCO/HCS/95.15 PART ONE: HIV/AIDS COUNSELLING What.is HIV/AIDS counselling? The Global Programme on AIDS (GPA) defines HIV/AIDS counselling as “a confidential dialogue between a client and a care provider aimed at enabling the client to cope with stress and take personal decisions related to HIV/AIDS. summary.text: Lists those who should receive HIV/AIDS counselling, including people with AIDS or HIV and their families, people seeking an HIV test and those worried about their risk. It also identifies others who may be involved, such as partners, household members and wider family.

sections.extract: Counselling for HIV/AIDS: A key to caring For whom should HIV/AIDS counselling services be provided? The clients of HIV/AIDS counselling services are likely to be any of the following: - people with AIDS and their families. - those who are HIV-positive, and their families; - those seeking, or agreeing to undergo, an HIV test; and - those who are concerned that they are at risk or have been at risk of acquiring HIV

summary.text: Continues the glossary, defining testing with and without informed consent, voluntary testing and mandatory testing. It advises against the term 'routine testing' because it does not say whether informed consent is sought.

sections.extract: Counselling for HIV/AIDS: A key to caring Testing with informed consent: HIV testing performed only after the client has given informed consent to it. Informed in this context means that in discussion (pre-test counselling) the client has been made aware of all the ramifications of HIV testing, including the risks and benefits, as well as of alternatives to such testing, in language he/she can understand. Consent
